title: Space reactor panel discusses SR-1 Freedom mission and design considerations
html:
At the 2026 ANS Winter Conference & Expo in Phoenix, Ariz., panelists in the session “Space Reactor Instrumentation and Controls” discussed Space Reactor-1 Freedom, which is aiming to be the first demonstration of nuclear propulsion in space, and what makes space reactors different from terrestrial reactors.

The panel featured Dianne Ezell, Space Reactor-1 Freedom lead and technical program manager for the Versatile Autonomous Lightweight Kilowatt-class Reactor Experiment (VALKRE) at Idaho National Laboratory; Frank Whitworth, deputy lead of the vehicle spacecraft on the SR-1 Freedom at NASA Johnson Space Center; and Brandon Wilson, R&D staff at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. It was moderated by Vivek Agarwal, instrumentation and controls lead on SR-1 Freedom at INL.

Unique constraints: While five reactors on Earth have conducted criticality testing this year, instrumentation and controls for space reactors require considering some key differences.

“In terrestrial reactors, you can just put tons of concrete and water around all of your reactor to stop radiation from getting out. In a space reactor, your limit is mass, and so every part of your I&C is going to get dosed,” said Wilson.

He said that while space-rated, radiation-hardened instrumentation exists, that technology is generally tested using a cobalt-60 source, which emits high-energy gamma rays, leaving an open question as to how it would hold up in a space reactor.

“No one ever puts neutrons on these,” he said. “I haven’t seen people publish data on putting a [programmable logic controller (PLC)] in a reactor before.”

Even cabling, Ezell said, becomes a unique problem, given that traditional cabling can’t be used in the space environment. “Cables are the heaviest thing we fly,” she said. For the SR-1 Freedom program, design has involved a process of bringing together nuclear expertise and space expertise and understanding “this new Venn diagram.”

Whitworth said one of the early conversations that had to happen within the SR-1 team was talking about data volume and onboard storage. Even if a large amount of data were collected through on-board sensors, only a limited amount could be sent back to Earth through the NASA Deep Space Network.

“I think an area that we can really work on is advanced computing on these spacecrafts,” said Ezell. “You don’t have to reduce sensors. You can handle it locally and only send the information that’s absolutely necessary.”

SR-1 mission: According to Ezell, the team will start up the SR-1 Freedom reactor once it’s in space, but before that, the reactor will be managed under Department of Energy standard DOE-STD-1271.

“That only goes through launch,” she said. Once SR-1 Freedom is on its way to Mars, “There is no regulator in space, and we can do a lot of things that we wouldn’t normally, so we can take some risks there.”

She said the plan is to start up the reactor as early as possible and then turn it back off until Skyfall has been delivered to Mars.

“It’s about seven days to start up this reactor with the power conversion system and go through all of the various checks,” said Ezell. “There will be a DOE reactor operator that sits right next to a NASA operator at [Johnson Space Center], and they will be starting up this reactor, going through various checkpoints.”

Post-Skyfall, the team plans to restart the reactor, using lessons learned from the first startup.

“Now our radiation limitations have been lifted off the spacecraft for the most part, and we can really drive this reactor, and so we can do things like purposely fail components to learn and get as much data as [NASA] will allow me to transmit,” said Ezell. “Diagnostics is going to be extremely important for us to decide if we restart the reactor and when we restart the reactor.”

SR-1 design and testing: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman previously described SR-1 as a “70 percent solution to prove that it works.” During the panel, Ezell described it as a C+ reactor that will collect data that can be used by industry to develop an A+ reactor.

“Good enough is good enough. That’s our motto,” she said.

Ezell said the team will be doing “extensive ground testing” of SR-1, including the development of an engineering demonstration unit and zero-power criticality testing, which will be done at INL.

The team also plans to test some of the project’s control hardware in the VALKRE system, said Agarwal, which he said is scheduled to go critical in the summer of 2027.

“We will be using flight systems to operate the reactor to the zero-criticality point,” he said.

Ezell declined to comment on whether SR-1 will be using a neutron source to start up the reactor.

SR-1 control architecture: Whitworth said the system will have some automation but will not be autonomous, which he said will be a goal for future missions.

Ezell said the team is leveraging experience from the Transient Reactor Test (TREAT) Facility.

“We will have scripts that go through various steps, but then they’ll have stopping points where it says, ‘Hey, are we ready to go to the next step?’ and then the human in the loop says yes or no,” she said.

Planning across missions: Agarwal asked the panel about creating instrumentation and controls that can be used across many missions, including those with different operational constraints, such as lunar reactor 1 (LR-1), which SR-1 is designed to support.

Ezell said key differences will be communications, autonomous controls, and life span. LR-1 will have far fewer restrictions in the amount of data it transmits to Earth, but it will be expected to run for at least 10 years, requiring autonomous systems and instrumentation with a long operational life.

“Supply chain is a huge issue,” she said. “This is the beginning of a long mission. After SR-1, there’s LR-1. After LR-1, there’s SR-2. NASA is already committed to these missions.”

Wilson said he doesn’t expect operational constraints to be a major factor.

“At the end of the day, every reactor kind of uses similar equipment. There’s nothing exotic out there, so I see it as—I don’t want to say one fits all—but it should be pretty much the same I&C for every type of mission,” he said.
